newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Resistance pledges to hold Cambodia frontline post.
newsitem.headline: Resistance pledges to hold Cambodia frontline post.

text.p: Khmer Rouge fighters have joined soldiers loyal to ousted Cambodian co-premier Prince Norodom Ranariddh to defend this outpost border village, Thai army sources said on Tuesday.
Both Thmar Don and O'Smach, some 40 km (28 miles) to the east, the last town under the control of Ranariddh's forces, were quiet on Tuesday morning.
The outposts are among the last significant pockets of resistance to the forces of Cambodian Second Prime Minister Hun Sen, who ousted Ranariddh in a coup over a month ago.

Thmar Don is in a small wedge of Cambodia's remote northwest on the border with Thailand where several thousand soldiers loyal to ousted Prince Norodom Ranariddh have withdrawn to make a stand against government forces under Hun Sen.
Fighters from the remnants of the Khmer Rouge movement are holed up in Anlong Veng, some 70 km (40 miles) to the east.

Ranariddh, barred from visiting the border area since his arrival in the Thai capital Bangkok last Saturday, has repeatedly denied his forces were cooperating militarily or politically with Khmer Rouge guerrillas.
Thmar Don, a village of a little more than 200 civilians, most of them women and children, is defended by a combined force of 500 Khmer Rouge and Ranariddh fighters, a Thai army source said.
"Some 300 Khmer Rouge soldiers from Anlong Veng arrived in Thmar Don in early August to help soldiers of Ranariddh fight Hun Sen," a Thai source who monitors the fighting told Reuters.
Cambodia's royalist guerrilla commander said his forces had enough ammunition to fight for four months but in the royalist-held outpost his men were almost out of bullets even before fighting began.
"We can defend this village even though we are now running short of food supplies and bullets," Colonel Nil Pin said.
For the more than 200 civilians in the village the safety of Thailand is just a few metres (yards) away if Hun Sen forces do attack. For them the shortage of food and malaria are bigger dangers.
"Four people died of malaria in the last five days," said royalist officer Colonel Chim Phiron.
Nearly 40 villagers were suffering from malaria. Four people died in the past week, Colonel Chim Phirun, a liaison officer with royalist forces said.
Chim said he was a security officer in King Norodom Sihanouk's palace in Phnom Penh before escaping with four colleagues two weeks after Hun Sen's bloody July 6 coup.
He said rival forces were facing each other at Prey Veng and Kiab villages about 16 km (10 miles) from Thmar Don.
He said the royalists would do their best to hold Thmar Don because he said it was one of the key frontline routes to O'Smach from the west.
For frontline troops under Hun Sen, 15 or 20 km (10 to 14 miles) to the south, the countless home-made mines and booby traps laid to block their advance are the biggest danger.

Government soldiers, many of them in their teens, were being trucked in to the area for an expected push on O'Smach but field commanders said minefields would have to be cleared before an assault on the royalist border town could begin.
Young soldiers in plastic thongs stepped gingerly up the dirt road, kicking at the dust every now and then at a suspected mine, witnesses said on Sunday. Not one metal detector was in sight.
Soldiers scraped at the red gravel with their fingers and marked detected mines with a bunch of leaves before moving slowing forward up the road.
Booby traps waited for anyone hoping to avoid the mines by stepping off the road and walking through the bush next to it.
Government soldiers say the home-made mines are made by the Khmer Rouge, "Pol Pot mines" they call them, after the notoroious guerrilla commander.
For a guerrilla force husbanding its ammunition supplies the devices are a cheap but highly effective way of stalling an advance.
Ranariddh, ousted by Hun Sen on July 6, denies that his forces are cooperating militarily with the Khmer Rouge guerrilla group.
But for government forces under Hun Sen on the frontline the home-made mines and boody traps are evidence enough that the two forces fighting Hun Sen are working together.
